title: Masoretic Pointing and Vowel Signs
description: Read the diacritic system that records vowels and pronunciation.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html: The vowel signs, called pointing or niqqud, are small marks written under, over, and inside the consonants to record the vowels. They were added by the Masoretes, Jewish scholars working roughly a thousand years ago, to preserve the traditional reading of a text that was written with consonants alone. The points are not original to the consonants and are not letters; they are a pronunciation aid. Learn each sign with its sound and read a pointed word as whole syllables, not sign by sign.

blocks.caption: The pointing system
blocks.html: The basic signs are a stroke and a dot in various positions. A short horizontal line under a letter is patah (a); a small T-shape is qamets (ā); three dots in a triangle are segol (e); two horizontal dots are tsere (ē); a single dot under a letter is hiriq (i); a dot above-left is holem (ō); three diagonal dots are qibbuts (u). Two vertical dots are shewa, which is either a very short vowel or silent.

blocks.caption: Reading pointed text
blocks.html: Read the consonant with its vowel together as one syllable, then move on. Because Hebrew writes the consonant first and the vowel around it, the eye must group them: the sign under ב is read with the ב. Practise on short words until the grouping is automatic, then longer words fall into place.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Do not confuse qamets (ā) with patah (a): the difference is length, not just shape, and it matters for syllables and grammar. Also keep qamets (ā) separate from qamets-hatuf, which is a short o that happens to use the same sign — a point taken up with syllables and shewa.
